pos.personaBrief: The core idea is keeping the ball among team-mates ('played excellently well together', 'adepts in passing the ball', 'working beautifully to each other's feet'), set against English individual dribbling. But it was an attacking 2-2-6 game that also used long kicks (The Field 1872), not modern possession-as-defence.

pro.personaBrief: Progression mixed 'long kicks, combined with a judicious plan of passing on' (The Field 1872) with short dribbles and 'vigorous rushes' (Glasgow Herald 1872). Alcock wanted 'much more than the mere passing on', so this is deliberate passing, but not patient short build-up from the back.

est.personaBrief: Forwards worked 'in pairs' (Arnott) and combined with each other rather than playing alone. The 2-2-6 'Box-Four' moved 'in step', so the shape was set, while the forwards joined up flexibly around the ball.

lar.personaBrief: Width is mixed: wing pairs went 'rushing down the wing and centring' (Arnott), but the 1874 goals 'came down the centre and the left' (SFHG). Wing play was done by passing pairs, not by lone dribblers, inside a six-forward line that always had wingers.

blo.personaBrief: The Scottish 'Box-Four' retreated 'in step, under pressure', and SFHG credits it with inventing defensive football against England's 1-1-8. With six forwards up the pitch, the front line still challenged the opponent, but chances came from combined moves, not from winning the ball high. Pressing itself is an evidence gap.

mar.personaBrief: The only hint is inference: the Scots 'paired up to stop the dribbling runs' (Wikipedia analysis), and the two backs held their positions ('magnificent play of the backs'). That reads as defending positions and the ball, with no dedicated man-markers.

pla.personaBrief: No verified evidence. From general knowledge, the combination game was a fixed principle Queen's Park and Scotland played every match ('Nothing succeeds better than... a combination game', Alcock), not a plan changed for each opponent. That fits the verified picture of a consistent team style.

res.personaBrief: This was an amateur, 'scientific' style that was also justified by success: Alcock's 'nothing succeeds better', and Scotland won 10 and lost 2 against England from 1872 to 1887. How the team played mattered alongside the result, and it played an attacking 2-2-6 with no substitutes and no shutting games down.

sis.personaBrief: The collective is the whole point. The lighter, slower Scots ('two stones' lighter, England had 'the advantage in pace') matched heavier individualists by playing together, and forwards worked in pairs while the English 'played an individual game'.

jog.personaBrief: The Scots were lighter and slower than England (Glasgow Herald 1872) and won through ball skill, 'dribbling and passing', and deliberate transfers of the ball rather than weight and 'heavy kicking'.

bas.personaBrief: Squads were built on Scottish-trained players: Queen's Park's young local amateurs, and Preston's imported 'Scotch Professors' (ten Scots in 1889). Neither academy development nor veterans as such were the guiding idea.

lid.personaBrief: There were no coaches. Queen's Park was a gentlemen's amateur club run by its members and captain, and Sudell at Preston was a do-everything 'trainer, masseur, groundsman, kit man'. Leadership was collegial rather than authoritarian, though the evidence is thin.
